newsitem.title: BELGIUM: EU parliament urges changes to takeover bids plan.
newsitem.headline: EU parliament urges changes to takeover bids plan.

text.p: The European Parliament on Thursday called for changes to draft framework rules on takeover bids in the European Union, which have also run into opposition from Britain's voluntary takeover panel.

The proposal, which aims essentially to guarantee protection for minority shareholders in the event of a takeover bid, is the European Commission's second attempt to harmonise member states' rules on takeovers -- a plan almost 10 years old.
Adopted by the Commission in 1995, the draft directive sets out guidelines for the conduct and transparency of takeovers, but leaves EU states the choice of how best to meet them.
Parliament, which has joint powers with EU ministers to decide on legislation affecting the EU's border-free market, approved the draft text but said it should be improved.
Euro-MPs said measures to protect minority shareholders should be triggered "as a result of an immediate or short-term acquisition" of control of a company.
Parliament said this would avoid legal uncertainty when the acquisition of a company's shares did not take place in a single operation.
Where national legislation provided for a mandatory bid as a means to protect small shareholders, the bid should be launched for at least 70 percent of all shares, Euro-MPs said.
The Commission's proposal refers only to 'a substantial part' of all holdings.
The EU assembly also set strict guidelines on the information to be provided to the employees of a target company, reflecting the belief that takeovers often result in job losses.

Workers or their representives should be informed within 24 hours of the bid being made public and be told by the bidder of any planned "changes to the terms and conditions of employment and any envisaged dismissals", parliament said.
In another key modification, Euro-MPs said the board of a target company should consult its employees before giving an opinion on the bid.
The Commission's draft directive is a much watered down version of its first proposal, made in 1989.

It does not interfere with well-entrenched corporate anti-takeover defences and accepts that self-regulating bodies like the UK takeover panel are just as able to protect small investors' rights as full-blooded legislation.
Unlike the 1989 proposal, the new directive no longer makes it compulsory for a party which has acquired one third of the voting rights in a target company to bid for 100 percent of the shares.

But the Commission's efforts have still failed to assuage the concerns of the UK takeover panel which has been lobbying hard for a non-binding resolution on the grounds that a binding directive would encourage disgruntled parties to engage in tactical litigation.

Internal market Commissioner Mario Monti told the parliament on Wednesday evening the Commission had tried to take into account British concerns and had proposed a formula which would cause little disruption to the British system.
"The directive as drafted is intended to keep the UK takeover system as intact as possible," Monti told Euro-MPs.
"(It) explicitly encourages voluntary control to be exercised by the supervisory authority in order to avoid recourse to administrative or judicial actions," he added.

Monti pointed out that tactical litigation in the form of judicial review was already possible in Britain but it was not a frequently used ploy "due to the reluctance of the English courts to intervene during a bid".
Equally, injured parties in Britain already had the right to sue for damages, Monti said.
The directive now goes back to EU ministers for consideration.
It is unclear when this will happen since the text has not even been examined by their technical experts despite the fact that it was sent to them over 18 months ago.
